# Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms: Origins, Pricing, and Global Impacts

The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) extends internal carbon pricing to imported goods to prevent carbon leakage and level the playing field for domestic industries [1]. As the EU moves into its definitive financial phase, other international jurisdictions are also developing or exploring similar border carbon pricing measures [3][10].

## Historical Origin and Primary Policy Objective of the EU CBAM

The EU formally adopted its CBAM in October 2023, transitioning to a system with binding financial obligations for importers in January 2026 [2][3]. The primary policy objective of the mechanism is to address the risk of carbon leakage, which occurs when production and its associated greenhouse gas emissions relocate from regions with stringent climate policies to jurisdictions with weaker or absent carbon constraints [1]. By mitigating this risk, the CBAM aims to preserve the industrial competitiveness of EU industries, prevent the undermining of unilateral climate action, and encourage cleaner industrial production in non-EU countries [1][3].

## Calculating Carbon Pricing for Imported Goods Under WTO Rules

To ensure compliance with World Trade Organization rules, the carbon cost embedded in imported goods is designed to be equivalent to the carbon cost borne by producers within the EU under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) [5]. Importers must report embedded emissions and purchase CBAM certificates to cover them [4]. The price of these certificates is tied directly to the EU ETS [3][4]. For imports in 2026, the European Commission applies a quarterly volume-weighted average of EU ETS auction clearing prices, shifting to a weekly calculation starting January 1, 2027 [4].

## Economic and Trade Impacts on Developing Nations and Major Partners

The implementation of the EU CBAM generates varied economic and trade consequences across the globe. Countries such as India, Russia, and Turkey face the sharpest declines in export competitiveness and economic losses [6]. For China, initial impacts are manageable, but export losses can rise significantly with CBAM expansion, and the policy worsens China's terms of trade [6][7]. Conversely, some of China's lost international market share flows to countries like India and ASEAN [7]. Studies show mixed real income effects; certain economies like the United States, China, Japan, the Republic of Korea, and India may experience aggregate real income gains, whereas others like the Russian Federation and Saudi Arabia experience losses [8]. Furthermore, the terms of trade for the United States show slight deterioration under certain modeled impacts [7].

## Development of CBAMs in the UK, Canada, and Australia

Following the EU's lead, other nations are actively developing or exploring their own carbon border adjustment mechanisms [3][9]. The United Kingdom is developing its own UK CBAM—designed separately from the EU version—set to go into effect on January 1, 2027, supported by newly published regulations on calculating the CBAM rate and carbon price relief [9][10]. Additionally, countries including Canada, Australia, Norway, and Taiwan are exploring or developing their own border adjustment approaches [3][9].

## Conclusion

Carbon border adjustment mechanisms are emerging as a core instrument in international climate policy to protect domestic industrial competitiveness and prevent carbon leakage [1][6]. While pioneered by the European Union through alignment with its Emissions Trading System [1][5], the framework is being replicated or explored by other major economies like the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia [3][10]. However, these mechanisms introduce complex economic shifts, affecting export competitiveness and terms of trade for developing nations and major trading partners alike [6][7][8].

research_notes.sub_question: How are other countries like the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia developing their own carbon border adjustment mechanisms?
research_notes.title: Global Default Values under the UK CBAM: Inaccurate, Ineffective, and Unfair | Climate Leadership Council
research_notes.content:
By Matt Porterfield

May 11, 2026

In less than eight months, the United Kingdom’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) goes into effect. A key design choice threatens to undermine the environmental integrity of the policy, induce more carbon leakage, and disadvantage cleaner firms—including U.S. manufacturers. More concerning, it would set bad precedent as other countries around the world develop their own border adjustment approaches. [...] More countries, including Taiwan, Norway, Australia, and Canada, are developing CBAMs and will make judgements about setting defaults that will impact U.S. producers. The UK has an opportunity to set a higher, fairer standard from the outset; global defaults would start the program out on the wrong foot.
